q: Your company runs the same containerized API in AKS clusters in three Azure regions. You want every cluster to pull images from a network-close copy while all pipelines keep using a single registry name such as contoso.azurecr.io/api:1.4. What should you do?
o: Upgrade the registry to the Premium SKU and add geo-replicas in the three regions
Create a Standard registry in each region and use az acr import to copy each image after every build
Keep a Basic registry and enable regional webhooks so each cluster is notified about new images
Enable zone redundancy on a Standard registry in the primary region
e: Geo-replication creates replicas of one registry in several regions behind a single global endpoint, and Azure routes each pull to the closest healthy replica. It requires the Premium SKU. Separate registries per region would need different login servers and extra copy jobs, webhooks only notify and do not replicate content, and zone redundancy protects against zone failures inside one region, not cross-region latency.

q: After a node scale-out, some AKS pods run a different version of your app even though every manifest references contoso.azurecr.io/web:latest. Which tagging practice prevents this?
o: Deploy with unique tags such as a build ID or commit SHA; keep stable tags for base images
Keep using :latest everywhere but restart every pod in the cluster after each new push
Use stable tags such as :1.0 for deployments and reserve unique tags for base images only
Delete untagged manifests after each push so that nodes can no longer pull old layers
e: Stable tags keep moving as new images are pushed, so nodes that pull at different times can get different images. Microsoft recommends unique tags for deployments and stable tags for maintaining base images. Restarting pods only hides the problem, swapping the two tag types is the opposite of the recommendation, and deleting untagged manifests does nothing about a tag that points to a newer image.

q: A production image contoso.azurecr.io/payments:2.3.1 must never be overwritten or deleted, even by users who have push rights. Which command should you run?
o: az acr repository update --name contoso --image payments:2.3.1 --write-enabled false
az acr repository untag --name contoso --image payments:2.3.1
az acr config retention update --registry contoso --status Disabled --type UntaggedManifests
az acr import --name contoso --source payments:2.3.1 --force
e: Image locking sets the write-enabled (and optionally delete-enabled) attributes on an image or repository so it cannot be updated or deleted. Untagging removes the tag and leaves an orphaned manifest, disabling a retention policy only stops automatic cleanup of untagged manifests, and import with --force would actually overwrite an existing tag.

q: Your Premium registry fills up with orphaned manifests every time a stable tag is re-pushed. You want the registry itself to delete untagged manifests after 7 days without running any task or script. What should you configure?
o: A retention policy for untagged manifests set to 7 days
An ACR task that runs acr purge --untagged --ago 7d on a schedule
A webhook that calls an Azure Function to delete old manifests
Content trust on the repository
e: A retention policy (a Premium feature) makes the registry delete untagged manifests automatically after the configured number of days, between 0 and 365. A scheduled acr purge task also works but is a task, which the requirement excludes. A webhook plus function is custom code, and content trust signs images and has nothing to do with cleanup.

q: You want to delete all tags in the repository samples/devimage that are older than 30 days, every day at 01:00 UTC, using only Azure Container Registry features. What should you use?
o: A scheduled ACR task (--schedule cron) that runs acr purge with --filter and --ago 30d
The registry's retention policy for untagged manifests, with retention set to 30 days
az acr repository delete, run manually from Cloud Shell at 01:00 each morning
Image locking on the repository with --delete-enabled true and a 30-day expiry
e: acr purge deletes tags and manifests by age and by repository/tag regular-expression filter, and running it as an ACR task with a timer trigger automates it. The retention policy only affects untagged manifests, so it would not delete old tagged images. A manual command is not automated, and the delete-enabled attribute only controls whether deletion is allowed.

q: A release pipeline deploys images by manifest digest (repo@sha256:...) instead of by tag. A teammate proposes a nightly acr purge task with --untagged to save storage. What is the main risk?
o: Images referenced only by digest can be deleted, so later pulls by digest fail
acr purge can't run inside an ACR task, so the scheduled job will fail every night
Purged images stay recoverable for 90 days, so storage usage won't actually drop
--untagged deletes every tag in the registry, including tags on locked images
e: Microsoft warns that systems pulling by manifest digest can break when untagged manifests are purged, because those manifests have no tag and match the untagged filter. Purge is commonly run as a task, deleted image data is unrecoverable rather than recoverable for 90 days, and by default purge skips artifacts whose write or delete attributes are locked.

q: Security policy requires that your container registry is reachable only through a private endpoint in your virtual network, with public network access disabled. Which SKU is required?
o: Premium
Standard
Basic
Any SKU, because private endpoints are free on all tiers
e: Private Link and public network access controls are Premium-tier features of Azure Container Registry. Basic and Standard provide the same data-plane APIs and Entra authentication, but they lack the advanced networking features. That is why the Premium tier is also required for geo-replication and other enterprise scenarios.

q: A build pipeline must push images to a registry, and a separate AKS cluster must only pull them. Following least privilege, which roles should you assign?
o: AcrPush to the pipeline identity and AcrPull to the AKS kubelet identity
Owner to the pipeline identity and Reader to the AKS kubelet (node) identity
Enable the registry admin user and share its password with both
Contributor to both identities at the resource group scope
e: AcrPush lets an identity push and pull, and AcrPull lets it pull only, which matches each workload exactly. Owner and Contributor grant management-plane rights far beyond what is needed, and Reader does not grant image pulls. The admin user is a shared credential intended for testing and is not recommended for headless services.

q: You built an image locally called orders-api:v1. Before running docker push to the registry contoso, what must you do?
o: Tag it with the login server name, such as contoso.azurecr.io/orders-api:v1
Rename the registry to orders-api so the registry and image names match
Run az acr build with the --no-push flag so the registry registers the local image
Add the label registry=contoso.azurecr.io to the image in the Dockerfile
e: Docker decides where to push from the image name, so the image must be tagged with the fully qualified login server name (<registry>.azurecr.io/<repository>:<tag>). Renaming the registry is unnecessary, az acr build with --no-push builds in the cloud without pushing, and a label in the Dockerfile does not change the push target.

q: Several teams share one registry and you want images grouped by team so access and cleanup are easier to manage. What is the recommended approach?
o: Use repository namespaces such as payments/api and search/indexer
Create one tag per team, for example api:payments and api:search
Store each team's images in a separate blob container of the registry storage account
Use a different Docker Hub organization for each team
e: Repository names can include namespaces (path segments), which group related repositories by team or product inside one registry. Tags identify versions of an image, not owners. ACR storage is managed by Azure and is not exposed as your own blob containers, and Docker Hub organizations are unrelated to your Azure registry.

q: Your builds depend on node:20-alpine from Docker Hub. To protect builds from upstream outages and rate limits, you want a copy of that image in your own registry without pulling it to a workstation first. Which command should you use?
o: az acr import --name contoso --source docker.io/library/node:20-alpine
docker pull node:20-alpine on a developer laptop, then docker push to contoso.azurecr.io
az acr repository update --name contoso --image node:20-alpine --write-enabled true
az acr build --registry contoso --image node:20-alpine --file Dockerfile.node .
e: az acr import copies an image from another registry (public or Azure) directly into your registry on the server side, with no local Docker engine involved. Microsoft recommends keeping copies of public base content in your own registry. Pull and push from a laptop works but depends on a workstation, repository update only changes attributes, and task logs only show build output.

q: The image contoso.azurecr.io/web has one manifest tagged both 1.7 and latest. You run az acr repository delete --name contoso --image web:1.7. What happens?
o: The manifest, its unique layers, and all its tags, including latest, are deleted
Only the 1.7 tag is removed; the manifest stays and latest keeps working
Nothing is deleted, because the manifest still has another tag (latest)
The image becomes untagged and is removed later by the registry's retention policy
e: Deleting by tag deletes the image itself: the tag, all unique layers referenced by the image, and all other tags associated with it. To remove only one tag and keep the image, use az acr repository untag instead. There is no protection for multi-tagged images unless the image is locked.

q: Which statement about Azure Container Registry service tiers is correct?
o: All three tiers share the same data-plane APIs and have zone redundancy by default where supported
Only the Premium tier supports Microsoft Entra authentication; Basic and Standard need the admin user
Webhooks are only available in the Standard and Premium tiers, not in the Basic tier
Zone redundancy is a Premium-only feature, and it must be enabled when the registry is created
e: According to the SKU documentation, all three tiers share the same programmatic capabilities and data-plane APIs, and all have zone redundancy enabled by default where regions support availability zones. Tiers differ in included storage, throughput, and advanced features such as geo-replication and private endpoints. Entra authentication and webhooks are available in every tier.

q: A developer has no Docker engine installed but needs to build the Dockerfile in the current folder and push the result to the registry contoso. Which command should they run?
o: az acr build --registry contoso --image app:v1 .
docker build -t contoso.azurecr.io/app:v1 . && docker push contoso.azurecr.io/app:v1
az acr import --name contoso --source ./Dockerfile
az acr repository update --name contoso --image app:v1
e: az acr build is an ACR Tasks quick task: it uploads the build context, builds the image in Azure, and pushes it to the registry, so no local Docker engine is needed. The docker commands require a local engine, az acr import copies existing images from another registry and cannot build from a Dockerfile, and repository update only changes image attributes.

q: You want every application image that is built FROM contoso.azurecr.io/base/dotnet:8 to be rebuilt automatically when the base image is patched. Which ACR Tasks capability should you use?
o: A task with a base image update trigger, with the base image on a stable tag
A quick task (az acr build) that each developer runs manually after patch day
A webhook on the base repository that deletes every dependent application image
A retention policy on the base repository with a short retention period
e: ACR Tasks discovers base image dependencies during a build and can retrigger the task when that base image is updated. To be tracked, the base image must use a stable tag such as dotnet:8. For base images in Azure container registries the run triggers immediately. A manual quick task is not automatic, deleting images does not rebuild them, and retention policies only clean up untagged manifests.

q: You must rebuild a maintenance image every night at 21:00 UTC even when no code changes. How do you create this task?
o: az acr task create with --schedule "0 21 * * *"
az acr build with --platform linux/amd64
az acr task create with --commit-trigger-enabled true only
az acr run with a YAML file stored in the repository
e: Adding --schedule with a cron expression to az acr task create gives the task a timer trigger. Timer-triggered tasks can still have source commit and base image triggers, and can be run manually. A commit trigger only fires on code changes, az acr build is a one-off quick task, and az acr run executes once rather than on a schedule.

q: You want an image to be built and pushed every time code is committed to the main branch of a GitHub repository. Which approach should you use?
o: az acr task create with a Git --context, a Dockerfile, and a Git access token
az acr build, run from a developer laptop after every commit to the main branch
A timer-triggered ACR task that runs every minute and checks the repository
A registry webhook on contoso that listens for git push events from GitHub
e: ACR Tasks supports source code commit triggers: when you create a task against a Git context with a personal access token, ACR registers a webhook in the source repository and runs the task on each commit. Manual quick builds are not automated, a per-minute timer wastes runs and adds delay, and registry webhooks fire on registry events such as push, not on Git commits.

q: You define build, test, and push steps in acr-task.yaml and want to run them once right now without creating a task. Which command should you use?
o: az acr run --registry contoso -f acr-task.yaml .
az acr task create --registry contoso --file acr-task.yaml
az acr build --registry contoso --file acr-task.yaml .
az acr task logs --registry contoso --file acr-task.yaml
e: Multi-step tasks are defined in YAML, and az acr run executes the file immediately as a one-off run. az acr task create registers a reusable task that runs on triggers. az acr build treats the file as a Dockerfile, not as a multi-step task definition, and task logs only shows output.

q: In a multi-step ACR task you want each build to get a unique image tag automatically. Which value should you use in the YAML?
o: The run ID variable, for example -t $Registry/app:$ID
The literal tag latest on every build
The Git branch name, so all builds from main share one tag
A random tag typed by the developer in the YAML before each commit
e: ACR Tasks exposes run variables, and the run ID ($ID in YAML, {{.Run.ID}} in task templates) is unique for every run, which is the documented way to produce unique tags. latest and a branch name are stable tags that get overwritten, and hand-typed tags are error-prone and not automatic.

q: A task named nightly-build already exists. You need to start it immediately for testing. What should you run?
o: az acr task run --registry contoso --name nightly-build
az acr task create --registry contoso --name nightly-build
az acr build --registry contoso --name nightly-build .
az acr task update --registry contoso --name nightly-build --schedule now
e: az acr task run starts an existing task manually, and every task can be run manually regardless of its triggers. Creating it again fails or redefines it, az acr build does not take a task name, and the schedule parameter expects a cron expression rather than the word now.

q: You must produce a container image for ARM-based edge devices, but your build agents are x64 machines with no emulation. What should you do?
o: Use ACR Tasks and set the target platform, for example az acr build --platform linux/arm64
Build on the x64 agent with docker build and push; Docker converts the image when ARM devices pull it
Enable geo-replication in a region that has ARM hardware
Set the WEBSITES_PORT setting to the ARM port
e: ACR Tasks provides cloud-based image builds for Linux, Windows, and ARM platforms, and the --platform option selects the target OS and architecture. Docker does not convert an image's architecture when it is pulled, geo-replication only replicates content, and WEBSITES_PORT is an App Service setting unrelated to builds.

q: An ACR task in registry contoso must pull a base image from a second private registry, fabrikam.azurecr.io. How should you give the task access?
o: Add a credential for fabrikam to the task with az acr task credential add
Enable the admin user on contoso so that tasks can sign in to any registry
Lock the base image in fabrikam with --write-enabled false so it can be read
Add fabrikam as a geo-replica of contoso so both registries share access
e: az acr task credential add stores a login for another registry (for example using a managed identity or username and password) so the task can authenticate during the run. Enabling the admin user on the task's own registry does not grant access to fabrikam, locking an image controls writes only, and geo-replication replicates a single registry rather than connecting two registries.

q: Your application images use FROM node:20 from Docker Hub, and base image triggers react slowly or are throttled. What does Microsoft recommend?
o: Copy the base image into an Azure container registry and build FROM that copy
Switch every Dockerfile to FROM node:latest so triggers track the newest image
Disable the base image trigger and rebuild all images weekly by hand instead
Set the task timeout to the maximum value so throttled pulls can finish
e: Microsoft recommends copying public base content into your own Azure container registry and building from that copy. This removes the dependency on the public registry, and base images in Azure container registries trigger dependent task runs immediately. Moving to latest makes builds less predictable, manual rebuilds lose automation, and a longer timeout does not change trigger behavior.

q: You want a task to build the image, run the unit tests inside the freshly built image, and push only if the tests pass. Which ACR Tasks feature should you use?
o: A multi-step task with build, cmd, and push steps
A quick task created with az acr build --no-push, then a manual push
A timer trigger that runs every five minutes
A base image update trigger on the test image
e: Multi-step tasks support build, push, and cmd step types, so you can run a container from the new image as a cmd step to execute tests. If a step fails the run fails and later steps such as push do not run. A quick build with --no-push cannot run tests, and triggers decide when a task runs, not what it does.

q: A scheduled ACR task failed last night and you need to read the build output of its most recent run. Which command should you use?
o: az acr task logs --registry contoso --name nightly-build
az acr repository show-tags --name contoso --repository app
kubectl logs nightly-build
az acr config retention show --registry contoso
e: az acr task logs streams or shows the logs of a task run; by default it shows the most recent run of the named task. show-tags lists tags in a repository, kubectl logs reads pod logs in Kubernetes rather than ACR task runs, and retention show only displays the retention policy configuration.
